sections.h2: What does an Ohio quitclaim deed actually transfer?
sections.html:
It transfers whatever interest the signer has, no more. R.C. 5301.02 says a grant of land conveys the entire interest the grantor could lawfully convey unless the deed clearly shows a smaller estate was intended. A quitclaim does not add anything to that: if the grantor owns half, the grantee gets half.

The Revised Code prints statutory forms for three other deed types, and each one carries named promises. The general warranty form in R.C. 5302.05 brings covenants that the grantor holds the land in fee simple, that it is free of encumbrances and that the grantor will defend title against all claims. The limited warranty form in 5302.07 narrows those promises to claims arising through the grantor. The fiduciary form in 5302.09 is for executors, administrators, trustees, guardians and receivers.

Those covenants arrive only when the deed says so. R.C. 5302.06 gives the words "general warranty covenants" the full meaning of the promises listed there. A deed without such words leaves the buyer relying on the title the grantor really has.

sections.h2: Who can witness the signing of an Ohio deed?
sections.html:
Ohio requires the grantor's signature to be acknowledged, and R.C. 5301.01 names the officials who can take it: a judge or clerk of a state court of record, the county auditor, the county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. That official certifies the acknowledgment over a signature of their own. Most owners simply visit a notary.

The statutory forms show what a tidy Ohio deed carries. Each names the grantor with marital status and county, recites consideration, gives the grantee's tax-mailing address, describes the land, cites the earlier recorded instrument by volume and page, and includes dower release language for a spouse. The sections reviewed print no separate quitclaim form, so the same elements make a sound checklist for any deed.

One duty trips up sellers of troubled houses. Under R.C. 5301.253, an owner who has received a written building or housing code violation notice must hand the grantee written notice of those violations before any transfer agreement is made, or before the deed is filed if there is no written agreement. A notice sitting on an issuing authority's public records also reaches later owners without a new order.

sections.h2: Where is a deed filed, and what does the recorder charge?
sections.html:
Filing happens with the recorder of the county that holds the parcel, as R.C. 5301.25 directs. Skipping that step leaves a hole: an unrecorded deed is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer who bought in good faith without any knowledge of it.

The recorder's price list sits in R.C. 317.32. The statute prints these items for recording and indexing a standard instrument:

  • Seventeen dollars of base fee and seventeen dollars of housing trust fund fee cover the first two pages.
  • Each page after that adds four dollars of each.
  • A county may tack on a preservation surcharge, capped at five dollars.

The auditor sees the deed first. If a surveyor drew the land, the auditor insists on the surveyor's name appearing in the deed, in a short sentence reading "A survey of this property was made by" and the name.

sections.h2: Who owes the Ohio conveyance fee on a quitclaim?
sections.html:
The party giving up title does. Under R.C. 319.202, the grantor covers the state-set fee plus any county transfer tax when the statement of value reaches the auditor. R.C. 319.54 prices the mandatory fee at one dollar or ten cents for each hundred dollars of value, using whichever is higher.

Counties may layer on a tax of their own. R.C. 322.02 allows up to thirty cents for each hundred dollars, charged to the grantor and handed to the auditor before the deed is taken to the recorder. Ask your auditor whether your county charges it.

How "value" is measured matters. For a sale it means everything paid, mortgage balance included. For a gift in whole or part it means the price the land would likely fetch on the open market. Misstating value on purpose is forbidden. A separate fifty-cent charge covers each transfer or entry on the auditor's books, paid by whoever asks for it.

sections.h2: Which Ohio transfers are exempt from the conveyance fee?
sections.html:
A good number are, and several match the transfers families make by quitclaim. When an exemption fits, the form needs only a note giving the reason.

Selected conveyance fee exemptions in R.C. 319.54(G)(3)
TransferStatute letter
To confirm or correct a deed already recorded(c)
Gift between spouses, or parent and child or the spouse of either(d)
Pursuant to court order, when not a result of a sale under that order(f)
Where no money or other valuable consideration is paid and it is not a gift(m)
Among heirs or devisees of one decedent with no money paid(s)
To a trustee when the grantor reserved an unlimited power to revoke(t)
On sale for delinquent taxes or assessments(e)

The list in section 319.54 runs longer, taking in government transfers, transfers that merely secure or release a debt, and assorted corporate and trust moves.

sections.h2: When do survivorship and transfer on death options beat a quitclaim?
sections.html:
For a family transfer meant to take effect at death, Ohio has statutory tools that a plain quitclaim does not match. R.C. 5302.20 creates survivorship tenancy when a deed or will shows clear intent that the survivor takes the whole. The word "or" between two grantees does not do it alone. A conveyance from fewer than all survivorship tenants to an outsider passes the grantor's interest only on condition that the grantor survives.

A transfer on death designation affidavit under R.C. 5302.22 lets an owner name beneficiaries who take title at death. It requires no payment and no handoff to the beneficiary. It does have to be on file at the recorder's office before the owner dies, at the same recording price as a deed, and it is sworn before someone authorized to administer oaths.

Two more survivorship rules affect family deeds. A conveyance from every survivorship tenant to another person, or from all but one of them to the remaining tenant, ends the survivorship tenancy and vests title in the grantee. And when the only two tenants are spouses and the marriage ends by divorce, annulment or dissolution, the title turns into a tenancy in common unless the judgment says the survivorship continues.

A quitclaim made now gives the grantee a present interest, and the conveyance fee exemptions in the table apply to family gifts. Whatever route is used, no deed clears taxes. The lien statute keeps the year's claim on the parcel until it is paid.

faqs.q: Can I use a quitclaim deed to sell my Ohio house?
faqs.a: Yes, any signed, acknowledged and recorded deed can carry a sale, but a quitclaim gives the buyer only the title you hold, with none of the covenants a warranty form carries. Ask your title company which form the buyer's lender will accept.

faqs.q: Does an Ohio quitclaim deed need to be notarized?
faqs.a: The signature must be acknowledged before one of the officials the statute names, and a notary public is on the list. Most owners use a notary.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed remove a mortgage or tax lien in Ohio?
faqs.a: No. The year's tax lien fastens on the first of January and sticks until paid, whoever holds title. Get payoff numbers from the treasurer and your lender before transferring.

faqs.q: Is there a conveyance fee on a deed between family members?
faqs.a: Gifts between spouses, and gifts from parent to child or a child's spouse, are on the exempt list. So is a transfer where nothing of value changes hands and it is not a gift. The form carries a short statement of the reason.

faqs.q: Where do I record an Ohio quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Take it to the recorder of the county holding the parcel once the auditor has endorsed it. Until then a later good faith buyer can prevail over it. Ask the recorder's office what it charges for recording.
